revolving_door.people: Trevor Brathwaite (Deputy Governor, April 2006 to September 2021; Saint Lucia's representative on the ECCB Board of Directors October 2002 to March 2006)
revolving_door.summary: The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank's own page on former governors and deputy governors gives Trevor Brathwaite's career. He is an accountant who spent about fourteen years in Saint Lucia's government, including Comptroller of Inland Revenue from 1995 and Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance from 2002 to 2006, sat on the ECCB Board of Directors as Saint Lucia's representative from October 2002 to March 2006, and was Deputy Governor from April 2006 to September 2021. The same page states that earlier in his career he worked for the accounting firms KPMG Peat Marwick, in Saint Lucia, New Zealand and Barbados, and Peat Marwick Mitchell and Co in Saint Lucia, and that he served on the boards of East Caribbean Financial Holding Co. Ltd and Jalousie (1996) Ltd. East Caribbean Financial Holding is a financial holding company. The page gives no dates for any of these roles and does not say whether East Caribbean Financial Holding, Jalousie (1996) Ltd or the accounting firms are privately owned or state-owned, so which side of his career is private is not characterised by this source. The page also records that he chaired the National Insurance Corporation Investment Committee and the Saint Lucia Air and Seaports Authority, both public bodies.
revolving_door.source_title: Former Governors and Deputy Governors (Eastern Caribbean Central Bank)
revolving_door.move: board seat at East Caribbean Financial Holding Co. Ltd alongside a career running into the ECCB deputy governorship; ownership not stated

revolving_door.people: T. Baswell Donaldson, CBE (first Governor and Board Chairman of the Central Bank of The Bahamas, 1 June 1974 to May 1980)
revolving_door.summary: The Central Bank of The Bahamas' own former-governors page states that T. Baswell Donaldson was appointed the first Governor and Board Chairman of the Central Bank on 1 June 1974 and served until May 1980. Before that he was Manager of The Bahamas Monetary Authority from 1968 to 1972 and its Chairman from 1972 to 1974, and he began his career as Assistant Secretary in the Ministry of Finance and later served as Controller of Exchange. The same page states that after leaving the Central Bank he chaired Commonwealth Bank, a Bahamian commercial bank, as well as the Securities Commission and the College of The Bahamas Council, and served as Ambassador to the United States. The central bank's page gives no dates for the Commonwealth Bank chairmanship beyond placing it after he demitted office in May 1980, and it does not say whether Commonwealth Bank is privately owned or state-owned. The Securities Commission and the College Council are public bodies. This is a different person from James H. Smith, whose record The Bahamas already holds.
revolving_door.source_title: Former Governors (Central Bank of The Bahamas)
revolving_door.move: from Governor of the Central Bank of The Bahamas to chairman of the commercial bank Commonwealth Bank; ownership not stated

revolving_door.people: Abdellatif Jouahri (Wali, i.e. Governor, of Bank Al-Maghrib from 2003; previously president of BMCE until 1995 and then president of the CIMR)
revolving_door.summary: Le Matin's report of 23 April 2003 on King Mohammed VI naming Abdellatif Jouahri wali of Bank Al-Maghrib sets out his career. It states he was president of BMCE, the Banque Marocaine du Commerce Exterieur, until 1995, the year the bank was privatised and taken over by Othman Benjelloun, after which he stepped back from business affairs; he was then appointed president of the CIMR, the Caisse Interprofessionnelle Marocaine de Retraites, and reworked it after a major reform; and he was then named wali of the central bank. Bank of Africa's own investor-relations page on its board of directors independently states that Banque Marocaine du Commerce Exterieur was privatised in 1995 and that the sale attracted a consortium of Moroccan and foreign institutional and financial investors led by Royale Marocaine d'Assurance. Neither source states that BMCE was privately owned during Jouahri's presidency, and both place the privatisation at the end of it, so on this evidence the BMCE side of his career was not private. The CIMR side is different. The official summary sheet published by Morocco's insurance and social-welfare regulator ACAPS, at https://acapsd10new.fornetmaroc.com/sites/default/files/fiche_synthetique_cimr.pdf, states that the CIMR was founded by a group of private-sector employers, was managed as an employers' association governed by the dahir of 15 November 1958 on associations, has governing bodies made up only of employer representatives, operates a voluntary scheme supplementary to the state social security system run by the CNSS, and converted into a societe mutuelle de retraite only in 2017 under Law 64-12. So the regulator's own text establishes that the CIMR was a private-sector employers' pension body, not a statutory public pension fund, at the time Jouahri led it immediately before taking the governorship. Le Matin gives no start or end dates for the CIMR presidency, so the commonly cited 2002 to 2003 span is not confirmed by these sources.
revolving_door.source_title: S.M. le Roi nomme M. Abdellatif Jouahri wali de Bank Al-Maghrib (Le Matin)
revolving_door.move: from president of the CIMR, a private-sector employers' pension body per the ACAPS regulator, directly into the governorship of Bank Al-Maghrib in 2003

revolving_door.people: B. Lkhagvasuren (Governor of the Bank of Mongolia from 22 November 2019; Deputy Governor 2016-2019)
revolving_door.summary: The Bank of Mongolia's own biography page for its Governor lists his full career, and it contains no commercial bank, asset manager, insurer or brokerage. The one move outside the Mongolian public sector is to and from the World Bank: the page states he was Regional Financial Management Advisor for Northeast Asia and the Pacific at The World Bank in Washington, D.C. from 1999 to 2000, immediately before returning to the central bank as Advisor to the Governor in 2000 to 2001. Everything else on the page is public: Researcher at the Economic Research Institution of Science 1989-1994, then Senior Economist, Director General of the Supervision Department and Director General of the Payment and Information Technology Department at the Bank of Mongolia, a seat on the Financial Regulatory Commission in 2002, Chief Executive Director of Mongolia's Deposit Insurance Corporation 2013-2016, Vice President of the Mongolian Bankers Association 2013-2016, Deputy Governor 2016-2019 and Governor from 2019. The Deposit Insurance Corporation is a public deposit-insurance body and the Mongolian Bankers Association is an industry association, not a private firm. This record is therefore flagged as a public move; no private-finance revolving door is evidenced for Mongolia.
revolving_door.source_title: Governor's biography (Bank of Mongolia)
revolving_door.move: from the World Bank in Washington into the Bank of Mongolia as Advisor to the Governor in 2000

revolving_door.people: Denny H. Kalyalya (Governor and Chairperson of the Board, Bank of Zambia, February 2015 to August 2020 and again since October 2021)
revolving_door.summary: The Financial Stability Board's published profile of Denny Kalyalya, who co-chairs its Regional Consultative Group for Sub-Saharan Africa, lists his career. It states he was Alternate Executive Director for the Africa Group One Constituency at the World Bank Group from 2010 to 2012 and Executive Director for that constituency from 2012 to 2014, and that he became Governor and Chairperson of the Board of the Bank of Zambia in February 2015, serving until August 2020 and returning to the post in October 2021. The profile also lists him as a Special Appointee at the International Monetary Fund, with no dates, and earlier as Director of Economics and then Deputy Governor for Operations at the Bank of Zambia, and as Head of the Economics Department and Assistant Dean of Post Graduate Studies at the University of Zambia. His outside board seat is at the African Export-Import Bank since 2019, which the profile does not classify. No commercial bank, asset manager, insurer or brokerage appears anywhere in the profile. This record is therefore flagged as a public move; no private-finance revolving door is evidenced for Zambia.
revolving_door.source_title: Denny Kalyalya, Co-Chair RCG for Sub-Saharan Africa (Financial Stability Board)
revolving_door.move: from Executive Director for Africa Group One at the World Bank Group into the governorship of the Bank of Zambia in February 2015
